01.r: Greek often puts the article before a personal name; English does not.

04.r: Jesus looks straight at the man before he speaks.
04.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to look at', and notes its use with a person in the dative, as a participle before a verb of speaking, as here. An aorist participle: the look comes first.

05.r: The man Jesus is speaking with.

06.r: Jesus loves the man, even as he tells him what he lacks.
06.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to love, to feel and exhibit esteem and goodwill to a person'. Neither Matthew's nor Luke's form of this saying has this clause.

08.r: Joins the speaking to the loving.

11.n: Greek has 'one' in the neuter, 'one thing', placed first for emphasis.

12.n: Literally 'one thing is lacking you', with 'you' as the object. The Textus Receptus has 'to you' instead, which the Geneva and DRC render.

13.r: Something still stands between the man and what he seeks.
13.n: Abbott-Smith derives the verb from a word meaning 'later' and gives its root sense as 'to come late, be behind', and metaphorically 'to come short, fail'.

14.r: The first of a string of commands.

15.n: Literally 'as many things as'. Abbott-Smith cites this verse for the neuter plural. Greek puts it before 'sell', as the YLT keeps it.

17.n: An aorist imperative: a single, decisive act.

18.r: Joins the giving to the selling.

19.r: Give the money from the sale.

20.r: The article; 'to' comes from the dative case of the noun.

21.r: Those who have nothing and depend on others.
21.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from a verb meaning 'to crouch, cower': first a beggar, then poor in general.

23.r: A promise attached to the commands.

26.n: Singular here, where Matthew's form has the plural.

28.r: A call to come to Jesus.
28.n: Properly an adverb, 'here, hither'. Abbott-Smith notes its use as an imperative, 'here! come!', and cites this verse.

29.r: A call to go with Jesus as his disciple.
29.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to accompany, follow', and as a figurative sense 'of discipleship'. A present imperative, which the YLT brings out with 'be following'.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus adds ἄρας τὸν σταυρόν, 'having taken up the cross', which is why the KJV reads 'take up the cross, and follow me' (the Geneva and YLT also have it; the DRC, ASV and BSB do not). It also reads σοί, 'to you', for σε, which the Geneva's 'is lacking vnto thee' reflects.
